questions.question_text: In a discharge tube, a beam is deflected toward a positively charged plate. What does this observation establish about cathode rays?
questions.option_c: They are electromagnetic waves with no charge
questions.option_d: They are neutral atoms
questions.explanation: Deflection toward the positive plate shows cathode rays carry negative charge; they were identified as electrons.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Cathode rays show the same charge-to-mass behaviour when the gas and electrode material in the discharge tube are changed. Which conclusion follows?
questions.option_b: Each gas creates a unique positive particle
questions.option_c: Electrons are common constituents of atoms of different elements
questions.option_d: The rays are made of the electrode metal only
questions.explanation: The invariant behaviour indicated that cathode-ray particles are universal components of matter rather than species-specific atoms.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: In Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment, most alpha particles passed through while a very small number were sharply deflected. Which model best fits both observations?
questions.option_a: Positive charge spread uniformly through a solid atom
questions.option_b: A tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus within mostly empty atomic space
questions.option_c: Electrons embedded in a neutral, indivisible sphere
questions.option_d: A nucleus occupying nearly the whole atom
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed through empty space; rare large deflections indicated a compact, massive, positively charged nucleus.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: To account for overall electrical neutrality, Thomson proposed that negative corpuscles were embedded in which part of an atom?
questions.option_a: Electrons fixed inside a negatively charged sphere
questions.option_c: A tiny positive nucleus with electrons in fixed energy levels
questions.option_d: Electrons embedded in a diffuse sphere of positive charge
questions.explanation: Thomson proposed a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, often compared to plum pudding.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Rutherford’s planetary model could not explain why orbiting electrons do not continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. Which later model addressed this problem for hydrogen-like atoms?
questions.option_a: Bohr’s model with stable, quantised orbits
questions.option_c: The kinetic theory of gases
questions.option_d: Dalton’s indivisible-atom model
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed stationary energy levels in which an electron does not radiate energy while remaining in an allowed orbit.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: In Bohr’s model, an electron in a stationary orbit remains in that orbit without continuously radiating energy. What feature of the model does this represent?
questions.option_c: A continuous range of allowed energies
questions.option_d: A nucleus with no protons
questions.explanation: Bohr’s stationary orbits have specified energies; radiation is associated with transitions between them, not motion within one orbit.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon and its electron moves from a lower allowed energy level to a higher one. Which condition must the photon satisfy?
questions.option_a: Its energy is independent of the levels
questions.option_c: It must have the mass of a proton
questions.option_d: Its energy equals the difference between the two levels
questions.explanation: Absorption occurs when photon energy matches the gap between allowed energy levels.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: An excited atom emits a photon as an electron falls to a lower energy level. Which relation is correct?
questions.option_a: Photon energy equals the initial-minus-final energy difference
questions.option_b: Photon energy is unrelated to the energy-level gap
questions.option_c: Photon energy equals the electron rest mass
questions.option_d: The electron absorbs energy from the nucleus
questions.explanation: The emitted photon carries energy equal to the difference between the higher initial and lower final levels.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Hydrogen produces separate spectral lines rather than a continuous range of colours. What is the best explanation?
questions.option_a: Only specific electron-energy transitions are allowed
questions.option_c: The nucleus emits every possible wavelength equally
questions.option_d: Electrons have a continuous range of stationary energies
questions.explanation: Quantised energy levels permit only certain transition energies, producing discrete spectral lines.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Compared with a proton, the mass of an electron is approximately:
questions.option_c: 1836 times as large
questions.option_d: 1/1836 as large
questions.explanation: An electron’s mass is about 1/1836 of a proton’s mass.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Which comparison between a proton and an electron is correct?
questions.option_a: The electron has no electric charge
questions.option_b: Their charge magnitudes are equal, but their signs are opposite
questions.option_c: They have equal masses and equal charges
questions.option_d: The proton is negative and the electron is positive
questions.explanation: A proton carries +1 elementary charge and an electron carries −1 elementary charge; their magnitudes are equal.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: An alpha particle is emitted during radioactive decay. What is its composition and net charge?
questions.option_b: One proton and one electron; charge 0
questions.option_c: One neutron; charge 0
questions.option_d: Two protons and two neutrons; charge +2
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus containing two protons and two neutrons, with a +2 charge.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A nucleus undergoes alpha decay. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
questions.option_a: Mass number decreases by 2 and atomic number by 4
questions.option_c: Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2
questions.option_d: Mass number stays fixed and atomic number increases by 1
questions.explanation: Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons, reducing mass number by four and atomic number by two.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: During beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus converts into a proton while emitting an electron. What happens to the parent nucleus?
questions.option_a: Atomic number falls by 1 and mass number falls by 1
questions.option_b: Both atomic number and mass number remain unchanged
questions.option_c: Atomic number rises by 2 and mass number falls by 4
questions.option_d: Atomic number rises by 1 while mass number stays the same
questions.explanation: Beta-minus decay changes one neutron into a proton; the nucleon count is unchanged, so Z rises by one and A stays constant.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A chloride ion is written ³⁷Cl⁻; chlorine has atomic number 17. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it contain, respectively?
questions.explanation: Protons = Z = 17; neutrons = 37−17 = 20; the −1 charge means one extra electron, giving 18.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A neutral sodium atom has electron arrangement 2,8,1. Which change gives it the stable electron arrangement of neon?
questions.option_a: It loses one electron to form Na⁺
questions.option_c: It gains one neutron
questions.option_d: It gains one electron to form Na⁻
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its single outer-shell electron to form Na⁺ with 10 electrons, matching neon’s electron arrangement.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Which set contains species with the same number of electrons?
questions.option_c: Na, Na⁺, Mg and Mg²⁺
questions.option_d: C, N⁻, O²⁻ and Ne
questions.explanation: Each member of O²⁻, F⁻, Ne and Na⁺ has 10 electrons; such species are isoelectronic.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Two atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Which statement is true about their neutral atoms?
questions.option_a: They have the same electron arrangement and usually similar chemical properties
questions.option_b: They must have different numbers of protons
questions.option_c: They have identical neutron numbers
questions.option_d: They are necessarily different elements
questions.explanation: Isotopes share proton number and, when neutral, electron arrangement; their chemical properties are therefore very similar.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Argon-40 and calcium-40 have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. What are they called?
questions.option_c: Isobars
questions.option_d: Isotones
questions.explanation: Isobars are nuclei of different elements with equal mass number but different atomic number.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons, while nitrogen-15 has 7 protons and 8 neutrons. What is their relationship?
questions.option_c: They are isobars
questions.option_d: They are isotones
questions.explanation: Isotones have the same number of neutrons but different proton numbers; each nucleus here has eight neutrons.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: An element occurs as isotopes of mass 35 u (75%) and 37 u (25%) in a hypothetical sample. What is its weighted-average atomic mass?
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: One unified atomic mass unit (u) is defined as:
questions.option_a: The mass of one hydrogen molecule
questions.option_b: The mass of one proton exactly
questions.option_c: One-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom
questions.option_d: One-twelfth the charge of an electron
questions.explanation: The unified atomic mass unit is one-twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom at rest and in its ground state.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: How many atoms are present in one mole of a pure element?
questions.option_c: Approximately 6.022×10²⁰
questions.option_d: Approximately 1.66×10⁻²⁴
questions.explanation: One mole contains the Avogadro number of entities, approximately 6.022×10²³.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A sample contains 0.50 mol of helium atoms. Approximately how many helium atoms does it contain?
questions.explanation: Number of atoms = 0.50×6.022×10²³ ≈ 3.01×10²³.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Using the Bohr shell-capacity rule 2n², what is the maximum number of electrons in the M shell (n=3)?
questions.explanation: For n=3, 2n² = 2×9 = 18 electrons.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: A neutral element has 17 electrons arranged in shells 2,8,7. Which element does the atom represent?
questions.option_c: Sodium
questions.option_d: Chlorine
questions.explanation: The atom has 17 electrons, so a neutral atom has atomic number 17: chlorine.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Radiocarbon dating relies on the fact that carbon-14:
questions.option_b: Has the same neutron number as carbon-12
questions.option_c: Is radioactive and decays at a predictable rate after an organism dies
questions.option_d: Has no electrons in a neutral atom
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 is radioactive; its decay after carbon exchange stops can be used to estimate the age of once-living material.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei and releases energy. Which explanation best accounts for the energy release?
questions.option_b: The nucleus absorbs energy from ordinary chemical bonds
questions.option_c: The products have slightly less total mass; the mass difference becomes energy
questions.option_d: The total number of protons vanishes
questions.explanation: The products’ total binding energy is greater; the small mass defect is released as energy according to E=mc².
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Class IX/ XI science references https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/iesc108.pdf

questions.question_text: Bohr’s simple model works best for hydrogen and one-electron ions but fails to predict spectra of many-electron atoms accurately. Which omitted effect is a major reason?
questions.option_c: Existence of a positive nuclear charge
questions.option_d: Repulsion between electrons
questions.explanation: The simple Bohr model neglects electron–electron interactions, which matter in multi-electron atoms and complicate their energy levels.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual verification: NCERT Physics, Atoms https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/leph204.pdf
